articles.title: Novas regras para doação de sangue no Pará; confira o que muda | G1
articles.standfirst: Pará adotará até o final de agosto novas regras. Mudanças federais tornam o processo mais inclusivo, reduzem tempo de espera para quem tem tatuagem e permitem doações de pessoas com mais de 70 anos.
articles.summary: Mudanças federais tornam o processo mais inclusivo, reduzem tempo de espera para quem tem tatuagem e permitem doações de pessoas com mais de 70 anos.
articles.body:
Fundação Hemopa já iniciou o processo de transição para as novas regras de doação no estado. — Foto: Marcelo Seabra/Agência Pará

Até o final de agosto, quem for doar sangue no Pará já deve encontrar um sistema mais moderno e humanizado.

Isso porque o Ministério da Saúde determinou, em nova portaria, mudanças nas regras de doação em todo o país.

A Fundação Centro de Hemoterapia e Hematologia do Pará (Hemopa) já iniciou o processo de transição para adotar as novas diretrizes.

Para o enfermeiro André Almeida, gerente da triagem de doadores da Fundação Hemopa, a atualização das regras irá aumentar os estoques de sangue em todo o estado.

"O impacto que isso vai causar será muito grande. Nós vamos conseguir trazer de volta doadores que antes ficavam inaptos.", destaca o gerente.

A nova regra deixa claro que a orientação sexual, identidade de gênero, atividade profissional ou condição socioeconômica não podem ser critérios de discriminação.

Além disso, o cadastro do doador agora deve, obrigatoriamente, respeitar o nome social de pessoas trans e travestis, garantindo a dignidade do cidadão desde a recepção.

Agora, os hospitais estão proibidos de exigir ou obrigar a doação de sangue de familiares para repor estoques utilizados por pacientes. O ato de doar deve ser estritamente voluntário.

Nenhum serviço de saúde poderá recusar atendimento médico ou constranger familiares devido à falta de doadores de reposição.

O peso mínimo exigido para a doação permanece em 50 kg. Em relação à frequência, os homens podem realizar até quatro doações por ano, enquanto as mulheres podem fazer até três.

A idade para doar também ganhou novas regras:

Primeira doação: Quem nunca doou pode iniciar o processo desde que tenha entre 16 e 60 anos (menores de 18 anos precisam de autorização dos responsáveis).

Doadores com mais de 70 anos: Agora, pessoas com mais de 70 anos que já são doadoras frequentes podem continuar doando, após passarem por avaliação médica.

Tatuagens, Piercings e procedimentos estéticos

Antes, quem fazia tatuagem precisava esperar até um ano para doar. Agora, o prazo de inaptidão para tatuagem, micropigmentação, maquiagem definitiva ou piercings é de 4 meses.

Se o uso da Profilaxia Pré ou Pós-Exposição (PrEP/PEP) foi por via oral, o tempo de espera para doar é de 4 meses após a última dose.

Se for utilizada a PrEP injetável de longa duração, o prazo de inaptidão é de 2 anos.

Com a nova regra pessoas que iniciaram relacionamento com um novo parceiro sexual, ou que tiveram múltiplos parceiros ocasionais nos últimos meses, ficam inaptas por 4 meses.

Vacinas Os prazos variam confirme o imunizante:

Covid-19 (tecnologia de RNAm ou vetor viral): 7 dias de inaptidão.

Febre Amarela e Tríplice Viral: 4 semanas.

A fisioterapeuta Yasmin Sousa é doadora há 10 anos. Para ela, as novas regras são fundamentais para atrair mais voluntários, sem abrir mão da segurança do processo.

Ela conta que sua trajetória na doação começou por uma necessidade familiar, em 2016.

"Sou doadora desde que minha avó adoeceu e precisou de sangue. Acredito que as novas regras vão facilitar a doação. A triagem continuará criteriosa, garantindo a confiança e a proteção de quem estará recebendo o sangue", afirma.

Yasmin Sousa, doadora há 10 anos, destaca que as novas regras vão facilitar o processo de doação no Pará. — Foto: Reprodução arquivo pessoal

Para quem ainda tem receio ou nunca doou, a Yasmin compartilha que o processo é rápido e indolor.

Muitas pessoas estão nos hospitais esperando por esse gesto e, em apenas alguns minutos, nós temos o poder de mudar o destino de alguém.”, reforça.

Para saber onde doar ou agendar uma doação, basta acessar o site oficial do Hemopa ou entrar em contato pelo telefone 0800 280 8118.

articles.title: Biocombustível de gordura residual: Ufam cria energia para aviões | G1
articles.standfirst: Pesquisa desenvolvida em Manaus já produziu biogasolina, bioquerosene, diesel verde e combustível para embarcações a partir de resíduos de caixas de gordura; próximo passo é ampliar escala e validar produtos.
articles.summary: Cientistas da Ufam produzem biogasolina e bioquerosene a partir de resíduos de caixas de gordura, transformando passivos ambientais em energia sustentável em Manaus.
articles.body:
Laboratório da Ufam transforma gordura descartada por indústrias e restaurantes em combustível para aviões e navios. — Foto: Divulgação/Ufam

O que normalmente seria descartado como resíduo pode ganhar uma nova utilidade na transição energética. Pesquisadores da Universidade Federal do Amazonas (Ufam) estão desenvolvendo uma tecnologia capaz de transformar gordura retirada de caixas de gordura de indústrias, restaurantes e shoppings de Manaus em biocombustíveis semelhantes aos derivados do petróleo.

A pesquisa, conduzida pelo Grupo de Pesquisa em Tecnologias Biossustentáveis da Amazônia (GP-TECBIOAM), já conseguiu produzir, em escala laboratorial, biogasolina, bioquerosene, diesel verde e um combustível equivalente ao bunker utilizado em navios . Além disso, o resíduo final do processo apresenta potencial para ser usado como ligante asfáltico na pavimentação de ruas e rodovias.

A tecnologia ainda está em fase de pesquisa e desenvolvimento e não está disponível para uso comercial, nem aprovado por órgãos reguladores. Os combustíveis foram produzidos e submetidos a testes em escala laboratorial, mas ainda precisam passar por novas análises e validação em laboratório credenciado. Segundo o pesquisador, a equipe trabalha atualmente para concluir essa etapa antes de avançar para testes em escalas maiores.

Coordenador do projeto, o professor Douglas Alberto Rocha de Castro, do Departamento de Engenharia Química da Faculdade de Tecnologia da Ufam, disse que a ideia surgiu durante um trabalho de conclusão de curso de um estudante de Engenharia Química.

“Percebemos que a gordura residual tinha potencial para ser convertida em biocombustíveis. A partir daí, submetemos um projeto à Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Amazonas, que foi aprovado, e conseguimos aprofundar as pesquisas para desenvolver tanto o processo quanto um catalisador próprio”, explicou.

Atualmente, cerca de 20 toneladas de gordura residual são geradas diariamente por indústrias do Polo Industrial de Manaus (PIM) e estabelecimentos comerciais da capital. Boa parte desse material é destinada à incineração, mas o grupo busca transformá-lo em uma fonte renovável de energia.

Antes de entrar no reator, a gordura passa por um processo de limpeza para retirada de água, areia e compostos que poderiam comprometer a reação química.

Depois, o material é submetido ao chamado craqueamento termocatalítico, processo semelhante ao utilizado em refinarias de petróleo. Nele, o calor quebra as moléculas da gordura em cadeias menores, formando um bio-óleo.

Segundo o pesquisador, de cada quilo de gordura processada, cerca de 700 gramas são convertidos em bio-óleo, um rendimento de aproximadamente 70%.

O diferencial da tecnologia, segundo Douglas Castro, está no catalisador desenvolvido pela própria equipe.

“Sem o catalisador conseguimos um produto com cerca de 50% de hidrocarbonetos. Com ele, chegamos próximo de 90%, o que torna o combustível muito mais semelhante aos derivados do petróleo”, afirmou.

Segundo a pesquisa, aproximadamente 20 toneladas de resíduos de caixa de gordura são coletadas diariamente em Manaus. — Foto: Divulgação

Após o craqueamento, o bio-óleo passa por uma destilação fracionada, processo semelhante ao das refinarias convencionais, que separa os diferentes combustíveis de acordo com a temperatura.

Bionafta, utilizada como matéria-prima na indústria petroquímica;

Biogasolina, que já apresentou parâmetros físico-químicos próximos aos exigidos pela Agência Nacional do Petróleo (ANP);

Bioquerosene, destinado à aviação, ainda em fase de aperfeiçoamento;

Diesel verde, considerado um dos combustíveis mais próximos das especificações convencionais;

Bio HFO (biobunker), equivalente ao combustível utilizado por grandes embarcações.

O material restante da destilação também ganhou uma nova aplicação.

“Essa fração pesada está sendo estudada como um bioligante asfáltico para pavimentação. Os testes já estão sendo realizados no laboratório de Engenharia Civil da universidade”, explicou o pesquisador.

Com parte das análises laboratoriais concluídas, o grupo iniciou os primeiros testes em motores a combustão.

A estratégia é avaliar inicialmente misturas entre gasolina comum e a biogasolina produzida pela equipe, sem a presença do etanol, para medir exclusivamente a influência do novo combustível sobre o desempenho e as emissões.

No futuro, os pesquisadores pretendem realizar testes também em motores a diesel utilizados em geradores de energia.

“O nosso objetivo não é apenas produzir combustíveis, mas transformar um passivo ambiental em energia. Isso pode beneficiar principalmente comunidades isoladas da Amazônia, onde a geração elétrica depende de motores estacionários movidos a diesel”, afirmou Douglas.

Laboratório da Ufam transforma gordura descartada por indústrias e restaurantes em combustível para aviões e navios. — Foto: Divulgação

Pesquisa começou na UFPA e ganhou força na Ufam

Douglas Castro conta que trabalha com biocombustíveis desde a graduação, na Universidade Federal do Pará (UFPA), onde também concluiu o mestrado e o doutorado. As experiências adquiridas ao longo da formação serviram de base para implantar a pesquisa em Manaus.

Desde que ingressou como professor efetivo da Ufam, em 2024, o projeto ganhou estrutura e novos equipamentos, permitindo ampliar os estudos.

Hoje, além do coordenador, participam da pesquisa professores dos departamentos de Engenharia Mecânica e Engenharia Civil da universidade, além de parcerias com a Universidade do Estado do Amazonas (UEA), UFPA, Instituto Militar de Engenharia (IME) e outras instituições.

Atualmente, os experimentos são realizados em reatores de bancada com capacidade para cerca de 200 mililitros de matéria-prima. A equipe já monta uma unidade semipiloto, que permitirá processar entre três e quatro litros por batelada.

O objetivo seguinte é construir uma planta piloto com capacidade entre 100 e 200 litros por ciclo, etapa considerada essencial para validar a tecnologia em escala próxima da industrial.

Para isso, o grupo busca novos financiamentos junto à Finep, Capes, CNPq e empresas instaladas no Polo Industrial de Manaus.

“Falamos muito em transição energética, mas cada região precisa encontrar sua própria solução. Na Amazônia, acreditamos que o caminho passa pelo aproveitamento dos resíduos da biomassa para geração de bioenergia”, concluiu o pesquisador.

Os resultados específicos da produção de biocombustíveis a partir da gordura ainda não foram publicados em uma revista científica. De acordo com Castro, parte dos resultados foi apresentada em congressos, incluindo um evento internacional realizado em Manaus, e outros trabalhos estão em processo de aprovação para apresentação.

O pesquisador informou ainda que o projeto financiado pela Fapeam passou por avaliação para a concessão dos recursos, mas ressaltou que esse processo não corresponde à revisão por pares dos resultados científicos. A equipe ainda trabalha na conclusão das análises antes de submetê-los à validação em laboratório credenciado.

articles.title: Motorista morre carbonizado após caminhão-tanque pegar fogo na MG-010 | G1
articles.standfirst: Motorista estava dentro do veículo quando o caminhão foi completamente tomado pelas chamas, em Vespasiano. Nenhum outro veículo foi atingido e não houve outras vítimas.
articles.summary: Motorista estava dentro do veículo quando o caminhão foi completamente tomado pelas chamas, em Vespasiano. Nenhum outro veículo foi atingido e não houve outras vítimas.
articles.body:
Um motorista morreu carbonizado após o caminhão-tanque que dirigia pegar fogo na MG-010, na altura de Vespasiano , na Região Metropolitana de Belo Horizonte , nesta quinta-feira (27).

Segundo o Corpo de Bombeiros, o veículo transportava combustível e foi completamente incendiado. O motorista ficou preso dentro da cabine e morreu carbonizado. As chamas eram tão intensas que o fogo podia ser visto de longe. Motoristas ficaram assustados e registraram algumas imagens logo após o acidente ( veja vídeo acima ).

Neste momento os trabalhos continuam no local e a rodovia segue interditada.

O Corpo de Bombeiros foi acionado para atender a ocorrência. O Batalhão de Emergências Ambientais e Resposta a Desastres (Bemad) também foi mobilizado.

Ainda de acordo com os bombeiros, nenhum outro veículo foi atingido e não houve outras vítimas. O rabecão foi acionado para fazer a remoção do corpo.

Carcaça do caminhão-tanque que tombou e pegou fogo na MG-10, em Vespasiano, na Grande BH. — Foto: TV Globo

articles.title: Simone Mendes no Barretão: cantora chora em retorno após 3 anos | G1
articles.standfirst: Cantora se emocionou logo no início da apresentação na madrugada desta quinta-feira (27) e depois colocou a arena para cantar uma sequência de hits.
articles.summary: Simone Mendes emocionou o público da Festa do Peão de Barretos com hits e um retorno marcado por lágrimas e aplausos após três anos longe da arena.
articles.body:
“A gordinha mais gostosa do Brasil chegou.”

Foi assim, com uma de suas frases mais conhecidas do meio sertanejo, que Simone Mendes anunciou o retorno ao palco do estádio de rodeios da Festa do Peão de Barretos na madrugada desta quinta-feira (27).

A cantora não se apresentava na arena do Barretão desde 2023 e precisou de poucas músicas para mostrar que estava com saudade. Depois de uma sequência com “Saudade Proibida”, “Erro Gostoso” e “Regime Fechado”, Simone parou no centro do palco e ouviu em silêncio os aplausos do público.

Simone Mendes fez show no Palco Estádio na madrugada desta quinta-feira (27) no Parque do Peão de Barretos — Foto: Ricardo Nasi/g1

O reencontro aconteceu três anos depois de uma passagem que também ficou marcada — mas por um motivo bem diferente.

Em 2023, Simone rasgou a calça durante a apresentação em Barretos. A cantora percebeu o problema ainda no palco, levou o perrengue com bom humor, amarrou uma blusa na cintura e seguiu o show.

Desta vez, o figurino voltou a chamar atenção, mas sem imprevistos.

Simone escolheu um conjunto branco formado por top e calça de couro, com amarrações e franjas inspiradas no estilo western. Chapéu de feltro cinza, luvas e joias completaram a produção.

Simone Mendes durante show na madrugada desta quinta-feira (27) na Festa do Peão de Barretos — Foto: Ricardo Nasi/g1

Mas foi quando começou a empilhar hits que a arena respondeu com mais força.

Com tem 12,4 milhões de ouvintes mensais só no Spotify, Simone é uma das cantoras sertanejas de maior sucesso no país. Ela colocou o público para cantar junto em uma sequência de parcerias que ganharam as plataformas digitais nos últimos anos.

Vieram “Manda Um Oi”, gravada com Guilherme & Benuto, e “Daqui Pra Sempre”, parceria com Manu Bahtidão.

Antes de um dos maiores sucessos recentes da carreira, Simone resolveu fazer uma pesquisa nada científica sobre quem estava curtindo a madrugada no Barretão.

“Quem trabalha amanhã? Quem parcelou levanta a mão. Quem está feliz levanta a mão”, brincou.

Em seguida, pediu que todos levantassem as mãos e repetissem: “Simone Mendes, hoje a noite vai ser a mais feliz da minha vida.”

Simone Mendes cantou seus grandes sucessos na madrugada desta quinta-feira (27) na Festa do Peão de Barretos — Foto: Ricardo Nasi/g1

Era a senha para “P do Pecado”, parceria com o grupo Menos É Mais. O hit foi recebido em coro pelo público e transformou a arena em uma das maiores cantorias da apresentação.

Também teve espaço para revisitar a história ao lado da irmã Simaria. Simone puxou “Meu Violão e o Nosso Cachorro”, um dos grandes sucessos da época da dupla, e ganhou mais uma vez a companhia do público.

Na sequência, vieram “Dois Tristes”, “Direitos Iguais”, “Esquecer Você” e “Louca”, mantendo a arena no embalo entre sofrência, romantismo e músicas para cantar em coro.

Simone Mendes no palco da Festa do Peão de Barretos 2026 — Foto: Ricardo Nasi/g1

O bom humor, uma das marcas de Simone Mendes no palco, também apareceu quando a cantora resolveu provocar os casais presentes na arena ao falar sobre sexo.

“Hoje tem, porque depois que casa é só uma vez na semana. Tem gente que é de mês em mês. E quem namora todo dia?”, perguntou. Ao ver algumas mãos levantadas, não perdoou.

“Um, dois, três, quatro, cinco... Mentiroso! Quando a gente namorava era um fogo desgraçado. Depois que casa... Mas, se o amor for verdadeiro, ele só aumenta”, brincou.

As risadas logo deram lugar à sofrência. Depois da provocação, Simone puxou “De Quem É a Culpa?”, um dos grandes sucessos de Marília Mendonça, e deixou parte da música por conta do público, que respondeu em coro.

Simone também acelerou o ritmo com músicas conhecidas do público. Entraram na sequência “Sonho de Amor”, na versão que ganhou projeção recente com Natanzinho Lima, além de “Seu Astral” e “A Hora É Agora”, de Jorge & Mateus, "Alô" e "Sinônimo", de Chitãozinho & Xororó.

Entre tantos sucessos, a cantora abriu espaço para novidade e apresentou “Quem Você Pensa Que É”.

A música conta a história de um casal que se separou e acreditava ter superado o fim da relação, até que um reencontro coloca os sentimentos à prova.

Simone Mendes deixou o palco após fazer uma oração fora do microfone, mas possível de se entender mesmo sem o som na caixa: "Eu te amo, Jesus!"

articles.body:
A saúde do rei Harald da Noruega , de 89 anos, deteriorou-se enquanto estava hospitalizado e seu estado agora é "muito grave" , informou a corte real nesta quinta-feira (27).

O monarca vivo mais velho da Europa e chefe de Estado cerimonial da Noruega desde 1991, Harald, foi levado ao hospital em 17 de agosto. O palácio informou que ele estava sendo tratado de uma infecção bacteriana no sangue.

O príncipe herdeiro Haakon e a esposa de Harald, a rainha Sonja, cancelaram todos os eventos planejados, informou o palácio em um comunicado.

Membros da família de Harald, incluindo o príncipe herdeiro e a rainha, foram vistos chegando ao Hospital Universitário de Oslo, onde o rei está sendo tratado, informou a mídia norueguesa.

O rei anunciou em 2024 que reduziria o número de atividades oficiais em que participa, levando em consideração sua idade, mas descartou a abdicação, afirmando que seu juramento como rei era vitalício.

articles.body: A Hollywood Hills house linked to the investigation surrounding the death of Celeste Rivas Hernandez has seen its monthly rent cut by more than $2,000, according to TMZ. The property, once rented by singer D4vd, is now sitting vacant after being placed on the market. The sharp reduction raises questions about whether the home’s connection to the high-profile case is making potential renters think twice before signing a lease.D4vd Hollywood Hills home gets major rent reductionThe property is reportedly now available for $21,500 a month, down from its earlier asking price of $23,950. Real estate records cited by TMZ show that the latest reduction came after the house remained on the rental market.The home became connected to the case after police investigated the property in relation to Celeste Rivas Hernandez’s death. Prosecutors allege that D4vd invited Rivas Hernandez to the house in April 2025 and that she was never heard from again.D4vd reportedly moved out in September 2025, shortly after police searched the residence. The house was later listed for rent in February, but it has apparently struggled to attract a tenant.The latest reduction came on August 16, when the asking price fell by more than 10 percent. It remains unclear whether the property’s association with the investigation directly caused the price cut.That uncertainty is important. A luxury home can remain vacant for many reasons, including its price, location, market conditions or a limited pool of potential renters. In this case, however, the property's history gives prospective tenants an unusual factor to consider.What happened inside the D4vd rental property?The Hollywood Hills residence has also figured into the evidence discussed during the investigation. According to TMZ, investigators used luminol at the property and examined residue found inside the home after obtaining a search warrant.TMZ previously reported that investigators found chainsaws, potential blood stains and a cut-up inflatable pool. Those items were cited as evidence during D4vd’s preliminary hearing. The significance of each piece of evidence remains a matter for investigators and prosecutors, rather than something that can be treated as proof of guilt on its own.The property has reportedly remained vacant since D4vd left. That adds another layer to the story as the owner continues trying to find someone willing to rent the expensive residence.For now, the house stands as an unusual piece of real estate caught up in a case that has attracted intense public attention. articles.body: LUCKNOW: Haryanvi singer and YouTuber Ankit Balyan, 32, was shot dead in a point-blank attack outside a gym in Shamli district on Wednesday evening, with preliminary information indicating that around 18 rounds were fired at him.The incident took place around 7 pm near Aryapuri Nala Patri in the City Kotwali area. Police said the attackers arrived on two motorcycles and opened fire as Balyan stepped out of the gym and headed towards his Scorpio SUV.Also read: Delhi model dies after being stabbed multiple times in abdomenAccording to police and eyewitness accounts, four assailants were allegedly waiting outside the gym. Balyan reportedly tried to shield himself by moving towards the co-driver's side of the SUV as a wall obstructed the driver's side.The attackers allegedly pulled open the vehicle door and fired repeatedly at close range. Five bullets reportedly struck Balyan in the head and abdomen, while three hit the front windshield of his SUV.Balyan was rushed to a nearby hospital, where doctors declared him dead on arrival. The attackers fled the scene, and police teams reached the spot soon after.Additional director general of police, Meerut Zone, Bhanu Bhaskar, reached Shamli along with senior officers to oversee the investigation. Superintendent of Police M P Singh said teams had been formed to identify and arrest the assailants.Police are examining CCTV footage from the gym and surrounding areas to identify the attackers and establish the sequence of events. Officials are also looking into a possible link to Haryana and investigating the motive behind the killing.The murder triggered protests by Balyan's family members, supporters and villagers. Protesters blocked the Delhi-Muzaffarnagar Road, around 50 metres from the shooting site, demanding immediate arrests and strict action against the accused.The situation became emotional after Balyan's body was brought to the road. His mother was seen holding her son's head in her lap and pleading with people not to disturb him, saying, "Don't speak, my son is sleeping."Balyan, a resident of Bantikheda village in Shamli, had more than 3.66 lakh YouTube subscribers and was known for his Haryanvi songs and performances. His videos often featured SUVs and firearms. He was also known for the song "Bhari Court Mein Goli Marenge Meri Jaan."He had attracted attention during a roadshow in Shamli in 2023, following which an FIR was registered against him and several supporters for alleged violations. There was also speculation that he was preparing to enter district panchayat politics, although police and his associates had not officially confirmed whether this was linked to the killing.Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav condemned the murder, alleging that the law-and-order situation in Uttar Pradesh had been reduced to "zero". articles.body: Raksha Bandhan is not merely a family celebration; traditionally, it is a sacred ritual representing protection, affection, responsibility and the strengthening of the sibling bond.In 2026, Raksha Bandhan will be observed on Friday, August 28 in India. The Purnima Tithi begins on August 27 and continues until the morning of August 28. For New Delhi, the reported Rakhi-tying muhurat is 5:57 AM to 9:48 AM on August 28, with Bhadra ending before sunrise. As timings can vary by location, families should refer to their local Panchang for city-specific calculations.Here are five things I recommend keeping in mind for an auspicious celebration.1. Prepare the Rakhi Thali MindfullyA traditional Rakhi thali may include the Rakhi, roli or kumkum, akshat, diya, sweets and other items according to your family’s traditions.The important thing is not extravagance but intention. Keep the thali clean and organised, and approach the ritual with a calm mind.2. Avoid Rushing the CeremonySince the auspicious window is in the morning, prepare everything beforehand. Keep the Rakhi, puja items and sweets ready so that the actual ceremony can be performed peacefully.The ritual should feel like a moment of connection rather than a hurried formality.3. articles.title: Japan’s Yayoi Kusama, global polka-dot art icon, dies at 97
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Yayoi Kusama, Japanese contemporary art icon known for her polka dots, died on August 14 at a hospital in Tokyo, her studio said Thursday. She was 97..
articles.body: Yayoi Kusama, Japanese contemporary art icon known for her polka dots, died on August 14 at a hospital in Tokyo, her studio said Thursday. She was 97.Kusama’s career spanned more than seven decades and crossed painting, sculpture, installations, performance, film and literature. Her repeated patterns, mirrored spaces and immersive installations eventually made her one of Japan’s best-known contemporary artists.Her studio said Kusama continued painting until her final days and would carry forward her wishes through art, bringing “hope and strength for the future” to people around the world, according to the Associated Press.Why did dots become Kusama’s defining language?Kusama traced her fascination with repeated patterns to hallucinations she experienced as a child, when she said she saw the world covered in spots.Those visions became a recurring element of her work. Polka dots appeared across her paintings, sculptures and installations, alongside nets, swirls and other repeated forms. Her mirrored installations further expanded the idea, using reflections, lights and repetition to create seemingly endless spaces.In a 2012 AP interview, Kusama said: “Polka dots are fabulous.”Repetition remained central to her work as she moved from paintings to sculptures and large-scale installations.Why did Kusama leave Japan for New York?Born into a middle-class family in Japan, Kusama wanted to pursue art despite pressure to follow a more conventional path. She left for the United States in 1957 and moved to New York, where abstract expressionism and action painting dominated the art scene.Her painstaking fields of repeated forms stood apart from the sweeping gestures and drips that were popular at the time. Kusama spent years struggling financially and received little recognition before her work began attracting wider attention.In New York, she became acquainted with artists including Andy Warhol, Georgia O’Keeffe and Joseph Cornell. She also staged anti-war “happenings” during the late 1960s, using painted dots and circles on human bodies and staging provocative public performances.Some participants were arrested for obscenity, while the performances brought further attention to Kusama’s work.Over the years, critics described her as Pop, avant-garde and feminist. Kusama, however, considered such labels inadequate for describing her art.How did Kusama become a global art icon?Kusama’s international reputation grew steadily in the later decades of her career, with exhibitions at major institutions including New York’s Museum of Modern Art and the Whitney Museum of American Art.Her works ranged from Macaroni Girl, a female figure covered in macaroni, to The Visionary Flowers, featuring giant sculptures of twisting tulips.Her mirrored installations became particularly popular, using reflections and repeated shapes to immerse visitors in environments that appeared to stretch endlessly.The commercial value of her work also grew. Christie’s auctioned one of her works for $5.8 million in 2008. In 2016, Japan awarded her the Order of Culture, one of the country's highest honours for artists.How did Kusama’s art enter popular culture?Kusama’s distinctive visual style eventually moved beyond museums and galleries.She collaborated with fashion brands including Louis Vuitton, while her signature patterns appeared on licensed products ranging from T-shirts and teacups to key chains.Her distinctive public image, including her orange bob-cut wig and patterned clothing, also became part of her global identity and was used in promotional displays.Kusama continued creating until the endKusama spent decades in and out of psychiatric institutions while continuing to make art. She repeatedly spoke about her determination to keep painting and creating.In her 2012 AP interview, she said she wanted to make “a thousand paintings, maybe two thousand paintings,” adding: “I will keep painting until I die.”She also described the act of creating as a process of discovery, saying she could pick up a brush and begin working without knowing exactly where the process would lead.After receiving Japan’s Order of Culture in 2016, Kusama said she was giving everything to her art so that people would “continue to be interested in my art, even after I am dead.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Google Cloud launches Gemini Enterprise to automate law firm workflows with AI agents
articles.summary: Tech News News: Google Cloud has introduced Gemini Enterprise for Legal, a new AI product purpose-built for law firms and corporate legal departments, aiming to autom.
articles.body: Google Cloud has introduced Gemini Enterprise for Legal, a new AI product purpose-built for law firms and corporate legal departments, aiming to automate complex legal workflows from contract review to regulatory compliance. The announcement, made Monday from Delhi and Sunnyvale, positions the offering as part of a broader push by Google into industry-specific AI tools, with Gemini Enterprise for Legal launching alongside a parallel version for financial services.Addressing legal-specific needsGoogle is framing the product as a direct response to the limitations general-purpose AI tools run into when applied to legal work — namely, an inability to reliably meet requirements like strict confidentiality, ethical walls between clients, verified legal authority, and complete data isolation. According to the company, trying to solve those problems by stringing together disconnected point solutions typically results in fragile, expensive-to-maintain workflows.Gemini Enterprise for Legal instead connects directly into a firm's existing document and matter management systems, automatically inheriting a firm's ethical walls in the process. Legal research generated through the platform is grounded in primary legal authority rather than relying solely on the underlying model's training data, and client data, playbooks, and negotiated positions are designed to remain permanently within a firm's private data perimeter.Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian said agentic AI gives legal professionals the ability to research case law, build arguments, and automate routine tasks in ways that create real value for clients, while stressing that accuracy and grounding in legal authority remain essential to that work.The four core componentsGoogle describes the platform as resting on four main pillars. The first is a set of purpose-built skills that guide AI agents through specific legal tasks, including legal brief drafting, citation verification, contract lifecycle management, regulatory horizon scanning, and fulfilling data subject access requests (DSARs).The second is a set of secure connectors, built using the Model Context Protocol, linking the platform to major legal industry systems including Docusign, Everlaw, iManage, NetDocuments, RelativityOne, Thomson Reuters, Harvey, Legora, and the Free Law Project's CourtListener database, among others.The third is a broader partner ecosystem of third-party legal tech providers and consulting firms building on top of the platform, including Accenture, Deloitte, and KPMG. The fourth is the underlying Gemini Enterprise platform itself, which gives IT and risk teams a centralized control plane with built-in audit logging, risk management, and governance.The workflows Google is targetingGoogle outlined several specific legal workflows it says the platform is designed to accelerate. On the compliance side, the system can proactively track legislative changes, court dockets, and regulatory activity, cross-referencing new developments against a firm's internal policies to flag potential exposure and draft updated policy language for attorney review. It's also designed to automate data discovery for privacy requests, compiling personal data scattered across enterprise systems to help meet DSAR deadlines with less manual effort.For transactional work, the platform benchmarks incoming vendor agreements, NDAs, and M&A documents against a firm's own playbooks, surfacing high-risk clauses so attorneys can focus their time on negotiation and judgment calls rather than first-pass review. It can also convert a firm's historical contract archive into a living, structured playbook by extracting key terms and fallback positions automatically. Additional targeted use cases include preparing and redacting court filings for motions to seal, and drafting NDAs with built-in structural and formatting consistency.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.summary: Tech News News: Nvidia has reportedly agreed to buy the open‑source AI model repository Hugging Face for $12.9 billion according to The Information. This deal would m.
articles.body: Nvidia has reportedly agreed to buy the open‑source AI model repository Hugging Face for $12.9 billion according to The Information. This deal would mark one of Nvidia’s biggest acquisitions to date and also underscores CEO Jensen Huang’s bet that demand for AI technology is still expanding rather than peaking. For those unaware, Hugging Face hosts open‑source large language models and datasets, giving Nvidia a powerful position at a time when rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI are exploring their own chip alternatives to Nvidia’s GPUs. The reported price tag stands in sharp contrast to Hugging Face’s annualised revenue of $150 million.Why Hugging Face matters to Nvidia's strategyAcquiring Hugging Face would give Nvidia control over one of the most important hosting platforms for open-source large language models and datasets, at a moment when builders of closed-source models — including Anthropic and OpenAI — are working to develop their own custom chips as alternatives to Nvidia's graphics processing units. Owning Hugging Face would give Nvidia a foothold deeper into the open-source side of the AI ecosystem, an area increasingly important as competition over chip dependency intensifies.A price tag far outpacing revenueThe reported $12.9 billion price stands in sharp contrast to Hugging Face's annualised revenue, which The Information reported earlier this week at just $150 million underscoring how much of the valuation is built on strategic and growth expectations rather than current earnings. Neither Nvidia nor New York-based Hugging Face immediately responded to Reuters' requests for comment outside of regular business hours.Nvidia's broader bet on AI demandThe Hugging Face report emerged the same day Nvidia forecast a 70% jump in revenue for its next fiscal year, reinforcing the company's confidence that AI demand remains on a steep upward trajectory. Nvidia also disclosed that it has $18 billion committed to equity investments through fiscal year 2027, part of its continued strategy of embedding itself financially across the AI industry rather than relying solely on chip sales.The deal follows a recent security scareThe acquisition report also comes about a month after Hugging Face was hit by a security incident in which an OpenAI model reportedly went rogue and triggered a hack that compromised Hugging Face's infrastructure — an episode that raised fresh questions about security risks tied to hosting and running third-party AI models at scale.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: A Perth homeowner hired agents to sell his house; a company they owned bought it for $705,000, their interest was disclosed six weeks later, and the homeowner later obtained an $800,000 valuation
articles.summary: Real Estate News: A  homeowner in Australia says he may have sold his Perth property for nearly $100,000 less than its value after discovering that the real estate agen.
articles.body: A homeowner in Australia says he may have sold his Perth property for nearly $100,000 less than its value after discovering that the real estate agents he hired to sell it were behind the company that bought it. Chao 'Jack' Wu sold the home for $705,000 in 2024, while a later valuation put its value at $800,000.Wu had signed an exclusive sales agreement with Ideal Realty WA on in April 2024, ABC News Australia reported. Six days after it, the agency told him it had received three offers, with the highest coming from a company called Generation Two PTY LTD.An email from agent Lynn Ding recommended that Mr Wu accept the offer, saying, “The buyer is almost a cash offer, we recommend to accept the offer and get it secure, or the buyer will offer another property.”Agent Roy Li also sent Mr Wu several messages, one of which said, “The buyer has no finance issue and we can accept it or the buyer will offer others after compared (sic).” Another said, “Will do the best to deal with the buyers. No worries”.Mr Wu said he signed the sale contract with Generation Two later that afternoon after negotiating an additional $20,000.Mr Wu became suspicious about the transaction after noticing that the buyer's name on the sale contract had been changed and later ordered corporate records from the Australian Securities and Investments Commission.Those records showed that it was Mr Li and Ms Ding who owned Generation Two. They also showed that the company had been established and registered at Ideal Realty WA's office address on the same day the offer was made on Mr Wu's home.Sale comes under scrutiny Mr Wu said that when he confronted the agents, they agreed to pay him another $10,000 and waive the agency's $10,000 sales fee. He said Mr Li sent him a disclosure form only after this, almost six weeks after the original sale contract was signed.In Western Australia, a real estate agent can buy a property from a client, but the agent must obtain the owner's prior written consent. According to Consumer Protection, the interest must be disclosed before negotiations take place so the seller can make an informed decision.Mr Wu said he continued with the sale because he believed he could face damages if he withdrew after signing the contract.He also alleged that Ideal Realty had held a 'ghost' open home intended 'to suppress his price expectations'.The day before the Generation Two offer was presented, Mr Li told Mr Wu that 13 groups had attended an open home and two private viewings had been booked. However, Mr Wu later found a Google review from a person who said they had arrived for a scheduled inspection and were told it had been cancelled.Mr Li rejected the allegation saying the tenant had refused to allow people inside the property, so potential buyers could only view the outside. “So many investors they don't need to see the property. They just check up the floor area; from the photos they can see the property condition,” he added.Agents deny non-disclosureMr Li denied that he and Ms Ding failed to tell Mr Wu they were the buyers before making an offer. When asked about his messages referring to 'the buyer', Mr Li said he could not remember the exact circumstances but believed he had spoken about himself in the third person because he was acting as both the agent and buyer. “Before the settlement, before we are doing the finance, before everything, he knows we're the buyer,” Mr Li said.However, he acknowledged that Mr Wu signed the written disclosure form weeks after the sale contract was signed. Mr Li initially said Mr Wu had refused to sign the form while negotiating for a higher price.Mr Li later told ABC, “The timing of the written disclosure was an administrative oversight, and our procedures have since been reviewed to ensure this does not occur again,” he said.Mr Li also explained why Generation Two was listed at a residential address on the sale contract instead of its registered address. He said the residential address was his postal address at the time.Property value questionedMr Wu later obtained legal advice and had the property retrospectively valued based on its value at the time of the sale. He said the valuation put the property's value at $800,000. The property had been sold to Generation Two for $705,000, meaning the valuation was $95,000 higher than the purchase price.Mr Li said he had also obtained a retrospective valuation. According to him, that valuation placed the property's value between $680,000 and $705,000. He said Mr Wu was disappointed because the market had changed and the property was worth more later. “He feels he lost money. But sorry man, that's your choice. You made a final decision,” he said.Mr Wu had bought the Kenwick property in 2020, after settling in Perth from China six years earlier. He had spent tens of thousands of dollars improving the 1970s brick-and-tile home, including renovating the driveway and adding a granny flat.After the sale, he complained to Consumer Protection, which investigated the matter and issued a formal warning to Ideal Realty WA over an alleged conflict of interest.A formal warning is issued when Consumer Protection believes there is a prima facie case that consumer law has been breached. Breaches can attract fines of up to $5,000 for individuals and $25,000 for companies.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: Brazil’s polluted Rio mangroves were disappearing under waste; then local fishers restored 18.2 hectares and more than 60 animal species returned
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Decades of pollution, untreated sewage, industrial activity and waste have placed heavy pressure on the mangroves around Rio de Janeiro’s Guanabara Ba.
articles.body: Decades of pollution, untreated sewage, industrial activity and waste have placed heavy pressure on the mangroves around Rio de Janeiro’s Guanabara Bay in Brazil. Yet in one of the bay’s remaining protected mangrove areas, local fishers and conservationists have been working to reverse the damage. Through Projeto UÇÁ, run by the Brazilian environmental organisation Guardiões do Mar, restoration efforts have helped recover 18.2 hectares of mangrove, while more than 64,500 mangrove seedlings have been planted. Monitoring of restored areas has also recorded more than 60 animal species, including birds, mammals and crustaceans. The work goes beyond planting trees, with local fishing communities involved in restoring habitats and removing waste from mangrove areas. The project shows how people whose livelihoods depend on coastal ecosystems can become important partners in restoring them, while the recovering mangroves provide habitat for wildlife and help strengthen the resilience of communities around Guanabara Bay.How Rio’s damaged mangroves began to recoverGuanabara Bay is one of Brazil’s best-known coastal environments, but rapid urbanisation and decades of pollution have severely affected parts of its ecosystem. At the northern end of the bay lies the Guapi-Mirim Environmental Protection Area, an important refuge for one of the largest remaining stretches of mangrove in the region. The protected area covers roughly 14,000 hectares and includes around 6,000 hectares of mangrove. Projeto UÇÁ was established in 2012 by Guardiões do Mar to combine mangrove restoration with scientific research, environmental education and community participation. Instead of treating local residents simply as beneficiaries of conservation, the project has involved traditional fishing communities directly in efforts to restore degraded mangrove habitat and protect the ecosystem on which they depend.Fishers became part of the restoration effortThe human story is one of the most distinctive aspects of the project. Artisanal fishers and crab collectors have worked alongside conservationists and researchers to restore mangroves, drawing on their knowledge of the ecosystem and its changing conditions. In areas where mangroves had been damaged, restoration teams used mangrove propagules and seedlings to encourage the forest to return. The cooperation also created opportunities for traditional communities to participate in environmental services and conservation activities. One such programme, known as Operação LimpaOca, involves removing rubbish from mangrove areas while providing payments to members of traditional communities. This means the people who rely on fishing and crab collection can also earn income from helping maintain the ecosystem, creating a direct link between conservation and local livelihoods.18.2 hectares of mangroves have been restoredSince the project began, restoration efforts have covered 18.2 hectares of mangrove, with more than 64,500 seedlings planted. The work has taken place over several years rather than through a single planting campaign, allowing restored vegetation to develop and become part of the surrounding ecosystem. One particularly important restoration area covers almost 10 hectares within the Guapi-Mirim protected area. According to Projeto UÇÁ, this restored mangrove has developed sufficiently to become visible in satellite imagery and has been monitored for signs of ecological recovery. The project is continuing its work, with its current phase running from 2024 to 2029 and plans to restore another 20 hectares between 2025 and 2028. This longer-term approach is important because mangrove restoration can take years to produce a mature forest capable of supporting a complex wildlife community.More than 60 animal species have been recordedThe most striking evidence of the restoration comes from the wildlife using the recovering habitat. Monitoring in a 9.9-hectare area restored in 2015 has recorded more than 60 animal species, including birds, crustaceans and mammals. Researchers have documented animals such as capybaras, lesser anteaters and coatis, while the endangered or threatened mangrove finch has also been observed in the restored landscape. The return and presence of wildlife provides an important indication that restored mangroves are beginning to function as habitat rather than simply appearing as newly planted vegetation. However, it is more scientifically accurate to say that more than 60 species have been recorded in the restored area rather than claiming that every species had disappeared and subsequently returned. The distinction matters because species may move between nearby habitats and use restored mangroves as feeding, breeding or shelter areas.The fight against waste continuesMangrove restoration is only one part of the conservation effort because waste remains a major problem around Guanabara Bay. Projeto UÇÁ’s cleanup work has removed more than 50 tonnes of solid waste from mangrove areas, preventing plastic, packaging and other rubbish from remaining trapped among the roots and waterways. The programme has involved traditional communities in collecting and removing waste, turning an environmental problem into an opportunity for local participation. Mangroves are particularly vulnerable to accumulated rubbish because their dense root systems can trap floating debris brought in by tides and rivers. Removing that material helps restore the physical condition of the habitat while reducing the risks posed to animals that live and feed there.The recovery of Guanabara Bay’s mangroves matters far beyond the trees themselves. Mangrove forests provide nursery habitat for fish and crustaceans, support birds and mammals, trap sediments and help protect coastlines from waves and storms. They also store significant amounts of carbon in their vegetation and waterlogged soils. For communities around the bay, healthy mangroves can therefore support both biodiversity and livelihoods. The work in Rio also demonstrates why conservation projects can be more effective when local communities are treated as partners. Fishers possess generations of practical knowledge about tides, waterways, wildlife and seasonal changes, while scientists can provide monitoring and restoration techniques. Together, those approaches have helped turn parts of a heavily pressured coastal ecosystem into areas where mangroves are growing again and wildlife is using the recovering habitat. The transformation is still ongoing, but the 18.2 hectares restored so far offer a measurable example of how damaged coastal ecosystems can be given a second chance.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. A team from the regulator is expected to conduct a detailed technical investigation to determine the cause of the crash. articles.title: Scientists built an AI robot that pretends to be an angry parent so that teachers can practise handling difficult conversations
articles.summary: Tech News News: Teachers can face difficult conversations with parents. Researchers at La Trobe University in Australia are trying to change that with an AI-powered t.
articles.body: Teachers can face difficult conversations with parents. Researchers at La Trobe University in Australia are trying to change that with an AI-powered talking robot called Fletch. The robot can take on the role of a disgruntled parent, allowing trainee teachers to practise responding to complaints, arguments and other difficult conversations in a controlled setting. According to an online report, Fletch can also change its responses based on what the teacher says, making each conversation feel less like a fixed script and more like a real interaction.The AI robot acts like a concerned or angry parentAs stated in the Phys.org report, Fletch has been programmed using insights from experienced teachers and their real-life interactions with challenging people in schools. Researchers interviewed teachers to understand the kinds of conversations they face with parents. The scenarios included a parent who is concerned about their child's falling grades and another who disputes their child's suspension.Fletch adopted different personas and recreated these situations with trainee teachers. The AI then responded to what the teacher says and can modify its reactions during the conversation. This allows teachers to practise handling situations that may become difficult or emotional.Teachers can practise before facing a real situationThe main idea behind Fletch is to give teachers a chance to make mistakes and learn in a safe environment before dealing with a similar situation at school. Lead researcher Therese Keane, a professor at La Trobe's School of Education, said verbal aggression has become a workplace concern for teachers in Australian schools.“Exposure to verbal aggression contributes to stress, burnout and difficulties in retention, further compounding teacher shortages,” Keane said. She added that trainee teachers and people entering the profession often receive little formal preparation for handling difficult conversations with parents.“This project addresses that gap by equipping preservice and early-career teachers with practical strategies and confidence to de-escalate challenging interactions,” Keane said.Fletch changes its reactions based on the teacher's responseUnlike a simple training video or a pre-written role-playing exercise, Fletch is said to be designed to interact with the person standing in front of it. It uses social cues, communication and behaviour to engage in a conversation. That means a teacher's response can influence how the conversation develops. The aim is to help teachers learn how to communicate clearly and calm situations before they escalate.Recently retired school principal Henry Grossek, who spent 57 years working in Melbourne classrooms, said he had seen verbal aggression against teachers increase over the years.“This is a skill that teachers new to the profession need to practice in a safe and nonthreatening environment,” Grossek said. “Fletch gives all teachers a chance to build their confidence and clear messaging before they get to the classroom.”Fletch will primarily be used to prepare La Trobe's preservice teachers before they begin working in classrooms. Several schools in Victoria have also signed up to use the system to train existing staff.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: In 1793, goats were introduced to Hawaii’s Kahoʻolawe; their population later reached about 50,000, and 200 years later the last feral goat was removed after severe vegetation loss and erosion
articles.summary: US News: From an island carved by voyagers, farmers and sacred traditions comes the unlikely story of thousands of hungry goats. They grew on Kaho’olawe from a.
articles.body: From an island carved by voyagers, farmers and sacred traditions comes the unlikely story of thousands of hungry goats. They grew on Kaho’olawe from a small 18th-century introduction into a herd of perhaps 50,000, stripping the vegetation and hastening erosion over the landscape. Today, the Hawaiian island is the focus of a decades-long effort to restore its ecosystems and cultural heritage. The story of Kahoʻolawe is one of environmental destruction, Indigenous activism and an ongoing effort to bring a sacred landscape back to life, states the Kahoʻolawe Hawaii govt website. According to the website, archeological evidence suggests native Hawaiians arrived on Kahoʻolawe around 400 A.D. Over the centuries the island became an important navigational center and supported fishing communities, agriculture, an adz quarry and places of religious ceremony. The cultural importance of the island is demonstrated by the some 3,000 archeological and historical sites and features that were documented through 2004. Kahoʻolawe, once a wahi pana and puʻuhonua, is a sacred site, a place dedicated to Kanaloa, the Hawaiian God of the ocean. But centuries of traditional use were followed by dramatic shifts. Scroll down to read the details.Introduction of goatsGoats were introduced to Kahoʻolawe in 1793, as a gift from Captain George Vancouver to Maui chief Kahekili. With no natural controls in place the population exploded. Cattle, sheep and goats were brought in when ranching began on the island in the 19th century. Uncontrolled grazing destroyed vegetation, and resulted in severe soil loss. By the late 1890s the island supported hundreds of cattle and some 15,000 sheep. Eventually the goat population alone was estimated at 50,000. The animals ate vegetation that would have helped to bind the island’s fragile soils in place. Loss of plant cover increased erosion that delivered sediment to surrounding waters and damaged the island’s watersheds.Ranch to bombing rangeThe military use added to Kaho‘olawe's environmental woes. After the attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941, the United States imposed martial law in Hawaii and began using Kahoʻolawe as a bombing range. In 1953 ownership passed to the U.S. Navy with the proviso that the island be returned in a habitable condition. Since the 1970s, Indigenous Hawaiian activists have opposed the bombing through occupations and legal actions. Their work helped raise awareness for the island’s cultural sites and environmental destruction. President George H. W. Bush had the bombing stopped in 1990. Congress later authorized the return of Kahoʻolawe to Hawaii and appropriated $400 million for the removal of unexploded ordnance.A long road to healingIn 1994, the navy transferred ownership to the State of Hawaii, which established the Kaho‘olawe Island Reserve Commission to manage the island. It took years to clear the ordnance. By 2004, about 75 percent of Kahoʻolawe had been surface-cleared, but big areas were still unsafe to enter without an escort. Another key element of the restoration effort was goat eradication. The last feral goats were removed after some 200 years on the island, removing a major source of grazing pressure and restoring the ability for vegetation recovery.Re-creating a living landscapeIncreasingly, restoration efforts have turned to watershed repair, erosion control, and re-establishment of native vegetation on damaged lands. State-supported conservation programs from 2004 to 2016 provided approximately $1.9 million in Clean Water Act funding, matched with about $1.9 million in volunteer restoration work. These efforts helped to restore targeted watersheds and reduce sediment runoff. Since 2013, the Aloha Kahoʻolawe program has also been working to establish sustainable funding for the island’s long-term recovery. The transformation of Kahoʻolawe is not yet complete. But the story of the island is beginning to change, from exploitation and environmental destruction to restoration and cultural renewal. Killing tens of thousands of goats was only a first step. The broader goal is to bring back a landscape where native plants can flourish, watersheds can recover, and Kahoʻolawe can once again be a place of cultural connection, learning and reverence.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: How burying straw helped China stabilise shifting desert sand and restore vegetation
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Explore how China stabilized shifting desert sands and restored vital vegetation using a simple technique of burying wheat straw. This innovative method has transformed an ecological crisis into a sustainable solution.
articles.body: On the eastern side of the Tengger Desert, the movement of sand hills was always a problem for surrounding villages and infrastructure. In the middle of the twentieth century, the wind blew through northwestern China, moving large amounts of sand and exposing the surrounding agricultural areas to dust storms. It became imperative to stabilise the sand hills once the Baotou-Lanzhou railway was constructed over the southeastern part of the Tengger Desert. Engineers realised that conventional planting techniques would not work on the shifting sand, as young plants would be uprooted by harsh gales or covered up by moving sand hills within a few days.To prevent the newly laid railway tracks from being permanently buried, scientists and local labourers turned to a simple material: wheat straw remnants. Instead of planting trees directly, workers used wooden shovels to press straw into the sand in a square grid. The technique altered wind flow across the desert surface.Decades after the straw checkerboard technique was introduced at Shapotou, researchers began studying the physical processes behind its effectiveness. A study published in the Journal of Arid Environments by G.Y. Qiu and colleagues examined how the straw checkerboard system affected wind flow, sand movement, and vegetation establishment.Qiu and his colleagues found that 1 m × 1 m straw checkerboards reduced wind-driven sand movement and helped stabilise dunes, with sand transport decreasing by up to 99.5% under the conditions examined. By stabilising the upper sand layer, the artificial barriers created conditions that supported vegetation establishment, including natural seed germination and later restoration efforts involving planted drought-tolerant speciesHow did the grid of straw turn into a living ecosystem?As the buried straw gradually decomposed, it added organic matter to the sand and improved its ability to retain moisture, creating conditions that supported biological soil crusts made up of mosses, lichens, and microorganisms. Once the sand surface stabilised, restoration efforts included planting drought-tolerant shrubs and native grasses within the protected squares.With the wind velocity suppressed and the sand motion halted, survival rates for planted vegetation increased sharply. The stabilised soil conditions enabled drought-tolerant shrubs, native grasses, and other vegetation to establish roots across previously shifting dunes. What began as an emergency measure to protect a railway line later evolved into a broader effort to control shifting sand and restore degraded desert landscapes.According to the researchers, the Shapotou case is seen as a good example of how arid lands can be managed and restored ecologically. The study indicates that, sometimes, cheap and simple methods may work in tackling the problem of environmental destruction. By combining the natural wind flow and using byproducts from agriculture, like straw, scientists have come up with a relatively cheap way that can be used in other arid regions.A long-lasting effect on desert restoration globallyResearch by Qiu and his colleagues found that straw checkerboards could support dune stabilisation and vegetation establishment over time, providing evidence of the technique's ecological effects. The results found by Qiu and his colleagues indicate that the straw checkerboard approach can be used to stabilise the shifting sand dunes and facilitate the establishment of vegetation in favourable conditions.The straw checkerboard approach has been modified for use in controlling desertification in other dry areas outside of China, such as North Africa and the Middle East. The Shapotou project highlights how simple engineering and restoration of vegetation can contribute to shifting sand stabilisation.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: France heatwave: 10 Nile crocodiles hatch on their own for the first time
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Ten Nile crocodiles have hatched entirely under natural conditions at a wildlife park in southeastern France for the first time, without any human int.
articles.body: Ten Nile crocodiles have hatched entirely under natural conditions at a wildlife park in southeastern France for the first time, without any human intervention or artificial incubation, after prolonged summer heat kept their nest warm enough for the eggs to develop.The hatchlings emerged at La Ferme aux Crocodiles in Pierrelatte. The park, which bills itself as Europe’s largest wildlife park focused on reptiles, normally relies on controlled incubation for crocodile eggs.Visitors spotted the 10 crocodiles hatching on Saturday and alerted park staff. The discovery initially brought excitement among visitors and the veterinary team, but that quickly gave way to concern over the conditions that had made the natural hatching possible.Samuel Martin, director of the reserve in Pierrelatte, told AFP on Wednesday: “For the first time, we had an incubation that took place entirely under natural conditions,” news network France 24 reported.Why is the natural hatching unusual?In the wild, Nile crocodile eggs incubate naturally in underground nests. Zoos, however, typically use carefully controlled incubators where temperature and humidity can be closely monitored.A Nile crocodile egg must be maintained at a constant temperature of 30°C-32°C for about three months for the embryo to develop and hatch.Martin said the “unprecedented natural process” behind the hatchlings’ birth was above all “a marker of climate change”.How did France’s heatwaves make it possible?France has endured three summer heatwaves and a record 52 days of extreme heat, conditions worsened by climate change.The prolonged hot weather created ideal conditions for the subtropical species to reproduce naturally. At the park, sand around the eggs retained heat accumulated during the day, keeping the nest warm enough for the incubation process to continue without human assistance.How are the 10 hatchlings doing?All 10 hatchlings are doing well. They will remain under close observation in the park’s nursery before being presented to the public.The successful hatching, however, has also raised questions about how the same unusually hot conditions may affect animals adapted to different climates.What could the heat mean for other species?Martin said species originating from “very hot countries are feeling comfortable”, while “species from more temperate environments may have suffered more”.The contrasting impact means the same prolonged heat that allowed a subtropical species to reproduce naturally may have been less favourable for animals accustomed to temperate conditions.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Housing First': How Sweden's Gothenburg is reducing homelessness
articles.summary: News News: Gothenburg, Sweden’s second-largest city, has seen a sharp decline in homelessness after adopting Housing First, a model that puts people into permane.
articles.body: Gothenburg, Sweden’s second-largest city, has seen a sharp decline in homelessness after adopting Housing First, a model that puts people into permanent homes before requiring them to address issues such as addiction or mental health.The city counted around 3,000 homeless people in 2026, including 411 classified as acutely homeless — those living on the streets or in shelters. Over the past decade, acute homelessness has fallen by about 60 per cent, while overall homelessness has dropped by just under 40 per cent.At the heart of the initiative is a simple principle: housing comes first. The programme provides people with permanent homes without requiring sobriety or other preconditions. Once housed, residents receive support for issues including substance abuse and mental health.“The idea is that your home should be a secure foundation to stand on, so that you can then work on your other problems in life,” said Borko Grujic, head of operations at Goteborgs Stadsmission, which runs the city’s Housing First programme, as quoted by AFP.For people who have spent years moving between shelters and the streets, having a fixed address can make a significant difference. Viking Weiner, 56, who previously struggled with addiction and homelessness, described his life before getting an apartment as “chaos”.“It’s so much easier when you have a home, a place of your own, to be able to relax and to be able to think about your own future,” he said.The model also changes the relationship between housing and addiction. A relapse does not automatically mean losing the apartment, with the programme following the same tenant protections as regular housing.The results suggest that the approach is helping people stay housed: around 80-90 per cent of those given apartments remain in them. The non-profit initially acquires the lease, with many residents eventually taking over the tenancy themselves after about two years.Gothenburg’s housing model has also gained national attention. Sweden adopted a long-term homelessness strategy in 2022 encouraging municipalities to use Housing First, although only 126 of the country’s 290 municipalities applied for grants to implement it.A key advantage for Gothenburg is its large stock of public housing, which makes it easier to secure apartments for the programme. The city began Housing First 14 years ago, making it one of the longer-running examples of the model.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: India vs China: How their nuclear-capable missile arsenals compare
articles.summary: News News: China and India, Asia's two most powerful countries, have spent decades building ballistic missile arsenals. These ballistic missiles are strategic we.
articles.body: China and India, Asia's two most powerful countries, have spent decades building ballistic missile arsenals. These ballistic missiles are strategic weapons that act as a deterrent, under the concept of Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD). This prohibitive concept states that two nuclear armed powers will not use these weapons on each other, as the use of such a weapon will ensure a retaliatory strike, thereby increasing the cost for the attacker. India and China's strategic missile arsenals now bear resemblance, but also at the same time there are differences in capability. The two countries also are also employing different philosophies for the use of these weapons, as the US Naval Institute states that China is building a significant amount of missile capability to hit US bases in the vast Pacific.While India is building its strategic missile arsenal to act as an insurance against attacks from nuclear weapons armed entities. This concept is enshrined in India's no first use policy for nuclear weapons. India depends on the Agni family of missiles for its land based nuclear deterrence, while China depends on the Dongfeng series.Indian and Chinese strategic missilesAt the shorter end of the spectrum, China's road-mobile DF-16 offers a range between 800 and 1,000 kilometres, giving it reach over Taiwan and much of the western Pacific. India's comparable system, the Agni-I, delivers a range of 700 to 900 kilometres, and while it lacks the DF-16's higher payload capacity of up to 1,500 kilograms, it remains a reliable, road and rail-mobile system tailored specifically for shorter-range contingencies closer to India's borders.Moving up the ladder in terms of range and capability, China's DF-21, one of the People's Liberation Army's most storied missiles, offers a range of up to 2,500 kilometres and famously spawned the world's first anti-ship ballistic missile variant, the DF-21D. India's Agni-II sits in a similar bracket, with a declared range of 2,000 to 3,500 kilometres, and has long been described as central to India's deterrence posture with respect to China, despite New Delhi's insistence that its missile programme is not aimed at any single adversary.At the intermediate range, China's DF-26, capable of striking targets over 5,000 kilometres away, including American bases in Guam, sits close in class to India's Agni-III, which offers a declared range of 3,000 to 5,000 kilometres and has been noted for a circular error probable of just around 40 metres, making it among the most accurate missiles in its class. This accuracy allows India to rely on smaller-yield warheads while still achieving high lethality, a design philosophy that keeps the system relatively compact for its range class.Where the comparison becomes genuinely interesting is at the intercontinental tier. China's DF-31A, a solid-fuel ICBM, boasts a range in excess of 11,000 kilometres. India's Agni-V, its first genuine intercontinental system, offers a declared range of 7,000 to 8,000 kilometres, though some Chinese analysts have suggested its true reach may extend closer to 8,000 kilometres once payload adjustments are factored in. Both missiles share canisterised, road-mobile configurations, a design choice that improves survivability and reduces launch preparation time.At the very top sits China's DF-41, believed to carry ten to twelve MIRV warheads across a range of 12,000 to 15,000 kilometres, making it one of the longest-range missiles in the world. India's answer, the still-developing Agni-VI, is expected to offer a comparable range of as much as 10,000 kilometres, with reports suggesting it could eventually be fitted with MIRV warheads and even a submarine-launched variant, mirroring China's own efforts to build a survivable, multi-domain nuclear triad.Taken together, the comparison suggests India has broadly kept pace with China across most range categories, even as Beijing continues to hold an edge in payload flexibility, warhead multiplicity, and the sheer scale of its overall missile inventory.

articles.body: From yoga to chakras and now “Lakshmi maxxing”, India’s ancient spiritual traditions have once again found an unexpected place in internet culture. But this time, the focus is on beauty, femininity, abundance and wellness all through the imagery of Hindu goddess Lakshmi.So, what exactly is Lakshmi maxxing? The word “maxxing” essentially means maximising or optimising a particular aspect of your life. Lakshmi maxxing takes the image and symbolism associated with goddess Lakshmi and turns it into a modern blueprint for improving one’s appearance, lifestyle, energy and sense of abundance.The trend has been popularised online by wellness mentor Lisa Power, who presented it as a way of bringing elements inspired by Indian traditions into everyday self-improvement. But the trend has received a lot of backlash from Indians. Those opposing it say Lakshmi is a revered goddess in the Hindu traditions and using it for just for an aesthetic trend is demeaning.Lakshmi is more than an aestheticIn Hindu tradition, Lakshmi is not simply a symbol of jewellery, beauty or an expensive lifestyle. She is a revered deity whose significance has developed over centuries within Hindu religious traditions and practices. She is associated with wealth and prosperity, but her symbolism is much broader. For many devotees, Lakshmi represents abundance, auspiciousness and well-being, with her worship forming an important part of religious and family traditions.When that symbolism is removed from its religious and cultural context and transformed into a collection of beauty tips, self-care rituals and aesthetic goals, questions naturally arise.Is a sacred figure being reduced to an internet aesthetic? Is an ancient tradition being repackaged as a wellness product? Or can people engage with the symbolism in a contemporary way without disrespecting its origins?Why the trend is attracting attentionPart of the appeal of Lakshmi maxxing is that it fits neatly into the language of modern wellness culture. Social media is already filled with ideas about “romanticising” everyday life, improving one’s appearance, creating rituals, attracting abundance and becoming more intentional about personal care. Lakshmi maxxing brings these ideas together under a distinctly Indian cultural image.Appreciation or appropriation?This is perhaps the most interesting part of the conversation. It would be too easy to assume that everyone using the term is deliberately appropriating Indian culture. Some people may genuinely be interested in Indian traditions and may see the trend as a way of reconnecting with cultural imagery and ideas. But cultural appreciation becomes more complicated when the original meaning of a religious symbol disappears.There is a difference between learning about a tradition and using its most visually attractive elements without understanding their significance. A deity worshipped by millions can mean something very different to a devotee than she does in a social media post about becoming more beautiful, luxurious or “high-vibration”.Why context mattersThere is nothing new about ancient traditions being adapted to modern life. Yoga, meditation and Ayurveda, for example, have travelled far beyond India and taken on new forms around the world. But when a religious practice or symbol enters mainstream wellness culture, something can be lost if its history is ignored.Lakshmi’s imagery carries meaning because of the traditions behind it. Her association with prosperity and abundance cannot be separated entirely from the religious and cultural practices in which those ideas developed. That does not mean every modern interpretation is disrespectful. It does mean that the more popular a trend becomes, the more important it is to understand what is being borrowed and where it came from.Lakshmi maxxing may eventually disappear like many internet trends do. But the debate it has started is likely to remain relevant.The real question is not simply whether Lakshmi maxxing is a passing wellness fad. articles.body: Long before Yellowstone National Park became known for strict rules around its hot springs and geysers, visitors were encouraged to marvel at some of the park’s unusual thermal features.One of them was Handkerchief Pool, a small spring in the Black Sand Basin. According to National Park Service, visitors could put a handkerchief into it and watch it disappear into the water. The item would then come back to the surface after being moved through the pool’s water currents. Vistors believed the items came back scrubed and clean.But visitors did not limit themselves to handkerchiefs. Over time, people began putting other objects into the pool. This gradually turned a natural thermal feature into a collection point for rubbish and other items and started to interfere with the pool’s natural activity.Handkerchief Pool’s activity eventually stopped in 1926. According to Yellowstone Science, a log was shoved into the pool’s vent, blocking the feature and stopping the movement of water that produced its unusual effect. Visitors, however, continued to throw objects into the pool even after it stopped working properly.The problem was not limited to the log. The pool had accumulated a large amount of material over the years. Objects that visitors had thrown into the water remained inside the feature, adding to the blockage and making it harder for the pool to function normally.Also, the park contains geothermal systems that depend on underground water movement, heat and narrow openings. Blocking those openings with foreign material can change or stop the natural activity of a spring. The damage was eventually investigated and a major cleanup was carried out in 1929.When Ranger Carlos Davis cleaned the pool in 1929, the amount and variety of material removed was astounding. More than one and a half bushels of debris were taken out of the spring.The debris included coins, more than 100 hairpins, nails, bolts, a horseshoe, a broken bottle, part of a spark plug, badges, nuts and about a dozen handkerchiefs.The 1929 cleanup helped improve the convection currents in the pool, but the work did not completely solve the problem. Records indicated that further work would be needed.Other springs and geysers were also affected when visitors threw rocks, coins, bottles and other objects into them. Minute Geyser in Norris Geyser Basin was among the most vandalised. It once erupted about once a minute, sometimes reaching 40 feet, but rocks and other material were repeatedly thrown into its vent. By 1969, the vent was clogged with rocks cemented together by mineral-rich spring water, causing the geyser’s activity to shift to a side vent. Its eruptions then became irregular and reached only a few feet.Morning Glory Pool in the Upper Geyser Basin was another heavily affected thermal feature. Before the road near it was diverted in 1971, visitors threw coins, rocks, logs, bottles and clothing into the spring. Repeated cleanups removed some of the material, but continued additions clogged the vent. The pool’s temperature may have fallen, allowing algae to grow, although Yellowstone geologists noted that natural causes may also have contributed to the change.The story of Handkerchief Pool did not end with the 1929 cleanup. In 1950, park geologist George Marler cleaned the spring again, removing the log and gravel that had washed into it. Water flowed into the pool once more, but the feature had been permanently changed by its long period of inactivity, with algae mats spreading onto its rims.Geysers and hot springs are relatively rare geological features and can be vulnerable to human activity. Many geysers around the world have been altered or lost because of geothermal energy development and tourism.
